origin: A garden selection of a species from the rocky hills of Turkey, the Caucasus and northern Iran
habitat: Wild ancestor grows on dry, stony hillsides and rocky slopes in full sun
blurb: The flat, purely silver lamb's ear — the one chosen when you want the foliage and nothing else. 'Silver Carpet' is the shortest of the family, a tight 3–6 in mat of thick, soft, unmistakably silver-white leaves, and it essentially never sends up a flower spike. That single trait is why it matters here: CSU Extension's own xeriscape groundcover guidance points gardeners toward the flowerless lamb's ears, because the flowering kinds seed themselves around and go untidy at bloom time. This one just stays a clean sheet of silver, which is what most people wanted from lamb's ear in the first place.
sun: Full sun; afternoon shade is welcome in the hottest, most reflective spots
water: Low; xeric once established — keep overhead spray off the wool, which traps water and rots
spread: Spreads by creeping stems that root as they run, forming a low mat; it does not flower, so it never self-sows
seasons: Silver-white woolly carpet from spring through fall, freshest in cool spring weather; no flower spikes to speak of; semi-evergreen — the mat holds through mild winters but browns and flattens in a hard one
wildlife: Wool carder bees (Anthidium spp.) shave the leaf fuzz to line their nest cells, so the foliage itself is a resource; with no flowers it offers no nectar, so pair it with a bee plant if that matters to you
deer: Deer and rabbit resistant — neither will touch the woolly foliage
toxic: Non-toxic to people and pets; not a culinary plant
gaps: Reel covers spring and summer only; no open-licensed fall or winter photo of this named cultivar exists. There is deliberately no flower shot — 'Silver Carpet' essentially never blooms, which is the point of the selection, not a gap.

care.hardiness: Hardy in USDA zones 4–8, which covers the Front Range (zones 5b–6a) with room to spare.[1] The foliage is evergreen in mild climates but deteriorates considerably in a harsh winter, so expect a flattened grey mat by late winter here that refreshes from the crown in spring.[1][2] The dense leaf wool doubles as sunscreen against our high-altitude light and slows water loss from the leaf surface.[2]
care.planting: Plant in spring once the soil has warmed, or in early fall so roots settle before the ground freezes; mid-May and early September are the two comfortable Front Range windows.[4] Set the crown level with the soil surface and keep mulch pulled back off it — a buried crown on a woolly plant is an invitation to rot. It grows well in containers and troughs, but a pot dries out and freezes much faster than open ground, so use a gritty free-draining mix and shelter the pot against a wall over winter.[1]
care.sun: Full sun produces the tightest, most silver mat.[1] It tolerates part shade and appreciates afternoon shade where summers are hot, but too much shade thins the mat and — more importantly — keeps the foliage damp, which promotes disease.[1]
care.soil: Average, dry to medium, well-drained soil.[1] Sharp drainage matters far more than fertility; lean ground gives denser, more silver growth than rich ground does. It handles the alkaline side of neutral without complaint, roughly pH 6.0–7.8, which suits Front Range clay provided the site drains.[1][2] Work in grit or plant on a slight rise if your soil is heavy and slow.
care.water: Dry to medium water — genuinely drought tolerant once established, and CSU rates lamb's ear as a xeric groundcover for this region.[1][4] Water at the base, never overhead: the woolly foliage traps moisture, and that is precisely what makes this plant susceptible to rot and leaf spot.[1] When in doubt, underwater it.
care.spacing: Space plants 12–18 in apart for groundcover use and let the creeping stems close the gaps.[1] In a still, enclosed bed leave a little extra room so air can move through the leaves.[1]
care.propagation: Division only. 'Silver Carpet' rarely produces flower spikes, so there is effectively no seed, and a named clone would not come true from seed in any case — it is propagated asexually.[1] Lift and split the mat in spring or early fall and replant rooted sections; the creeping stems root as they go, so rooted pieces separate easily.[1] Divide every few years when the middle of the patch thins or goes woody.[3]
care.feeding: Skip it. Lamb's ear colours up best and stays densest in lean soil; feeding produces soft, floppy, rot-prone growth.[2]
care.maintenance: Very low maintenance.[1] The one job worth doing is raking out the dead matted leaves in early spring before new growth pushes through, which is the difference between a silver carpet and a grey mess.[3] Pull mulch back off the crowns, and cut out any brown rotted patches after a wet spell so air can reach the soil. Divide when the centre of the mat thins.[3]
care.troubles: Rot and leaf diseases in humid or wet conditions are the main problem; the woolly foliage traps moisture, so well-drained soil and base watering are essential.[1] Boulder's dry air works strongly in your favour here — this plant fails far more often in humid climates than in ours. It can also spread aggressively, so give it a hard edge or expect to trim it back from neighbours each spring.[1] Slugs and snails occasionally shelter under the mat in a damp season.
care.companions: A workhorse edging and foliage accent for borders and rock gardens.[1] The flat silver reads beautifully against roses, bearded iris, catmint and sedums, and it is the safer choice than the flowering kinds anywhere you do not want a groundcover seeding itself around.[4]

edible.summary: A foliage groundcover, not a food plant — no part of lamb's ear is eaten.[1][3]
edible.caution: 'Silver Carpet' lamb's ear has no culinary use and no part of it should be eaten. It is not considered poisonous — lamb's ear is not listed as toxic to people, dogs, cats or horses, so a child handling or stroking the leaves is not a worry[3] — but not poisonous is not the same as edible, and no authority documents any food use for the leaves, flowers or roots.[1][3] The soft, absorbent leaves of lamb's ear were historically used as an improvised dressing for cuts and scrapes, which is occasionally misread as a food or herbal-tea tradition; it is neither. Do not confuse this ornamental with the culinary mint-family herbs it loosely resembles.
